description: AllpaNina (Quechua for “earth” and “fire”) merges NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one consistent long-term record. VIIRS sees more fires than MODIS, so joining them creates a false jump. We calibrate VIIRS per Peruvian department with a fixed factor κ (2013–2022), validated and tested once on reserved data: WAPE drops from 4.30 to 0.31. The site offers a monthly calendar and map for Peru, and lets anyone process any region in the browser with NASA FIRMS files.
summary:
AllpaNina, derived from Quechua words for "earth" and "fire", is a web platform that integrates active fire detections from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS sensors into a consistent, long-term record. While MODIS has tracked fires for over 20 years, its mission is nearing its end. VIIRS detects a higher number of fires due to its smaller pixel size; consequently, the two time series cannot be combined directly without creating an artificial jump in recorded fire activity.

This is the rationale behind AllpaNina: we calculate a calibration factor, κ, for each department in Peru—based on data from the 2013–2022 period—and apply it as a fixed parameter. We then validate this factor using new data and conduct a specific test on a reserved dataset. For Peru, this reduces the weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE) from 4.30 to 0.31.

The web platform provides a monthly calendar and a map of thermal anomaly activity for Peru and its 25 departments. Furthermore, users can process data for any region worldwide by uploading files from NASA FIRMS directly through their web browser. The algorithm is designed to be reproducible, and its limitations are stated transparently: a detection does not necessarily equate to a confirmed fire.

AllpaNina is significant because it enables the analysis of long-term fire trends without conflating a change in satellite sensors with an actual change in conditions on the ground.
details:
AllpaNina is an interactive web platform that transforms open data from NASA FIRMS into a coherent, long-term record of satellite-observed thermal activity in Peru and across the globe. By integrating observations from the MODIS and VIIRS sensors, spanning from January 2013 to July 2026, the platform enables users to explore historical patterns through interactive calendars, maps, and analyses covering all 25 departments of Peru.

A key challenge is that MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities, which makes direct comparisons between their observations less than fully reliable. To address this, we developed a methodology that aggregates detections into "cell-day" units and performs regional calibration of VIIRS observations against those from MODIS, using independent periods for training, validation, and testing. Furthermore, the "My Region" feature allows users to apply this same processing methodology to other parts of the world, directly from their own computers.

The goal of AllpaNina is to support scientific research, environmental monitoring, and preventive planning by providing accessible, transparent, and reproducible historical data. While it is not intended to replace early-warning systems or predict forest fires, the platform offers valuable scientific context for understanding how satellite-observed thermal activity varies across different regions and over time.

AllpaNina is built with Python (NumPy, pandas, Shapely, pyproj, PyArrow) for the reproducible scientific pipeline, and React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and MapLibre GL for the web platform. In “My Region”, all processing runs locally in the user’s browser. AI assistants were used to support coding and data analysis; this is documented in AI_USE.md in the project repository.
